newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal parliament to meet on test motion next week.
newsitem.headline: Nepal parliament to meet on test motion next week.

text.p: Nepal's King Birendra has summoned parliament to take up a communist-backed no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's coalition government, state-owned radio said on Tuesday.
The palace issued a statement read on Radio Nepal saying the monarch had called the special session of parliament for 1 p.m. (0715 GMT) on December 16.

On Sunday, 11 breakaway deputies of the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), holding a crucial balance of power in parliament, announced they were withdrawing support for Deuba's 15-month-old coalition government.
Seven of 13 RPP ministers resigned from Deuba's 46-member government.
The RPP faction accused Deuba of harassing its activists and breaking an unspecified pledge to the coalition partners.
The three-party coalition has controlled 108 seats in the 205-seat lower house, where Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress party has 86 lawmakers.
The RPP, considered close to the monarchy, has 19 seats and the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP) has three members.
But the opposition United-Marxist-Leninist (UML) party, with 87 deputies, has joined the 11 breakaway RPP lawmakers and had asked the king to convene parliament to take up the motion against Deuba.
To topple Deuba's government, his opponents would need at least 103 votes in the 205-seat House of Representatives.
The communists and rebel RPP faction claimed they control at least 102 votes and would win over more deputies.
"We are confident that the no-confidence motion will be passed," UML general secretary Madhav Kumar Nepal told Reuters.
The UML said the motion would be registered against Deuba's coalition on Tuesday or Wednesday. A vote on the motion cannot be held until at least 10 days from the date it is registered.

The UML and RPP rebels have the support of two independent deputies and claim the backing of two NSP members. But the NSP disputes that claim and says only 10 RPP deputies had switched sides, reducing the strength of Deuba's opponents to 101 votes.
Political analysts said the three deputies from the leftist Nepal Workers' and Peasants' Party (NWPP) could settle Deuba's fate.
The NWPP considers itself a revolutionary party and in the past has not voted with the UML.
Violent demonstrations against King Birendra's absolute powers led to the establishment of multi-party democracy in 1990 in the Himalayan kingdom, one of the world's 10 poorest nations.

Mid-term elections in late 1994 yielded a hung parliament. The UML won the largest number of seats and formed a minority government that lasted until September 1995, when Deuba's forces pushed through a no-confidence motion.
The next parliamentary elections are not due until 1999.
In March, six RPP ministers resigned from the administration, but they patched up their differences with the government in time for Deuba to survive a no-confidence motion.
